answer:
1. The animation shows a grid of historical US starting periods. It builds the grid from FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates, and the image labels it "illustrative." Each cell is a scenario. A light cell means the buyer was ahead after ten years, and a dark cell means the renter was ahead. Almost every cell is light. A thin dark stripe runs down the middle.

2. The grid itself stays the same across the six frames. What changes is the on-screen text. Frame 1 has only the legend. Frames 2–4 add a caption, "rent tag 6%: buyer ahead in 92.2%." Frames 5–6 add a second caption, "the share moves with the rent you assume." In frames 5 and 6 the first caption drops out. The dark stripe shifts slightly from frame to frame, but I can't tell whether that's meaningful or just perspective or camera motion.

3. Under the 6% rent assumption, buying beat renting over ten years in about 92.2% of the historical windows, and renting won in the rest. The share of buyer wins depends on the rent growth or rent level you assume. A different rent assumption would give a different percentage. The footer says "US only · history, not a forecast," so the figure describes the past and doesn't predict what will happen.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might infer that buying has usually come out ahead over ten years. They would also take away that this depends on the rent assumption and isn't guaranteed. The caption, "the share moves with the rent you assume," tells them to check the result against their own local rent.

5. The animation didn't state any advice. The idea that buying has usually won comes from the captions and the grid. Any suggestion to act on it, or to test your own rent assumption, is my own reading. The one thing it says directly is that the result is sensitive to the rent assumption, and that it is history and not a forecast.
